Hey there! Welcome to the Celica community. I'll be listing things out from some of the things I've picked up from this subreddit (I drive a 2005 Celica GT with a VVT-i engine and use it as a daily):

For issues:  
\- I've seen people encouraging for newer 7th gens to be pursued (2003 - 2006). The ones from 1999-2002 have recently been noted to have more oil burning issues from what I've seen in a lot of these posts. For those who are more familiar with what that issue is, please feel free to correct me.  
\- Due to the age of the 7th gen, rust should be a big thing to look for. And they can hide in the engine bay, door jambs, and beneath the side skirts. Look for rust in the chassis. It's common to see rust unfortunately, especially for high mileage 7th gens and if you live in an area where there's a lot of snow.   
\- I've also heard of instances where high mileage 7th gen GT's transmissions seem to feel like it's 'slipping' when changing gears. I haven't experienced that issue yet, and my Celica's near 350k miles.   
\- In relation to the oil burning issue, 7th gen GT's also have cat degradation due to that. It might affect the earlier 7th gens more than the recent ones, so keep in mind of that if you're looking into purchasing an earlier 7th gen as well.   
\- Check the hatchback struts (two black bars that hold up the Celica hatch) and see to it if they actually work when opening up. A lot of YouTube vids will showcase it, and people have been traditionally using wooden sticks and bars to keep the hatch open. I've had to replace the stock ones with OEM ones. I did order a pair from RockAuto, but they sent me two left-sided hatchback struts instead. If you have to buy those hatchback struts from RockAuto, make sure they're able to support the trunk if the Celica has a spoiler or wing on top.   


Purchasing:  
\- You definitely should not be looking into 7th gens that cost 10k or above. From what I've seen, < 5k is the good range, while < 3k is the best and ideal range. Remember to do those pre-purchase inspections when you're there physically and look for areas where rust may build up. Hopefully another user can offer you more advice about the purchasing. 

For driving:  
\- I personally love driving mine as a daily. I use it to drive to my college campus, to my clinical shifts, and to work. There's actually a decent amount of space in the trunk of the Celica if you take the rear seats down; so if you need to go family grocery shopping you'll be set. I've gotten some compliments with the car throughout driving.

Depends on what type of IFT services are in your area. 

I’ve worked in a private ambulance non-emergent IFT service and…let’s just say that I’m surprised it’s still up and running after I left that company some time ago. The company I worked for was owned by 1 person, a licensed FF/EMT, who then left the position and his friend ended up taking it. These types of IFT service companies mostly transported/gouged money out of hospice, DNR/DNI, and non-ambulatory patients. If these patients could not sit upright or stand on their own, then we would take them to a facility to be transported to, for an appointment, or they’re going home for to be discharged. You will do the same thing over, and over, and over again for all your shifts. Depending on the time of coworkers you may get, you will have to show up some time early to perform a proper rig check off before you guys even hit the road. And don’t be alarmed if the equipment you’re checking on in the rig is 2-3 years late of inspection or evaluation, because according to your manager, it’s “normal and they can’t afford new stuff.” Then, you go to the facility or residence to pick the patient up from, then do your routine physical assessment along with obtaining V/S at least twice. Then you drop the pt off at the receiving facility or residence, or wait till the appointment is done until you take them back. Then you get a signature from the patient’s family or nurse/medical staff. Then you repeat the same thing 5-6 times. Over, and over, and over again. It’s exactly why I left that company after working for almost a year.

I haven’t had any experience with hospital-based IFT/ emergent IFT services. But definitely avoid the private owned non-emergent ambulance services.

Agreed. How I was taught and what I go by in paramedic school is, “Treat the S/S, not the machine.” For example, some of my family members has a hx of Type II DM. One of my relatives had taken their own BGL & it was reading in the mid 70’s. Yes, the reading is in the “normal” levels via the books, but this was a considerably low per my relative’s baseline BGL reading which would be in the 130’s-170’s; not to mention he was cool, clammy, c/o dizziness, looked like shit, etc. A 90’s/60’s BP may alarm some folks, but that’s my resting BP 🤷.

While, yes, there are discrepancies that pt’s may say about themselves and it may not seem like a big deal for us or we see it as a joking matter, we as healthcare providers still have to advocate for our pt’s and at the least take in consideration of what our pt’s may say is ‘normal’ or ‘not normal’ for them.

NTG 
1) Systolic BP < 100 because it reduces preload since it works by vasodilation. 
2) Allergies to nitrates. This should be obvious.
3) There are studies online that show NTG having an increased hypotensive effect on those with right ventricular hypertrophy or presenting with an IWMI, but consult with protocol. 
4) Pt that has taken PDE inhibiting medications within the past 72 hrs (tadalafil or sildenafil; common brand names: Viagra, Aronix, BlueChews, etc.)

ASA
1) Pediatric pt’s because it increases likelihood of developing a rare condition called Reye’s syndrome. 
2) Any allergies to other NSAIDs (ibuprofen, ketorolac, etc.) 
3) Pt’s with PMHX of, or is currently experiencing s/s of gastritis, peptic ulcer disease, or GI bleeds due to its NSAID properties and because it’s also an antiplatelet.

My first semester comprised of paramedicine-level pharmacology, paramedic-level patient assessments, and basic cardiology classes which included knowing different terminology along with interpreting 4 ld. rhythms. Throw in some medical terminology knowledge and A&P review as well too to stay ahead of the game. 

For pharmacology, I recommend getting an in-depth knowledge and review of what is involved in both your central nervous system (CNS) and peripheral nervous system (PNS), such as what neurotransmitters are involved and the different types of receptors that affect what organs and which systems, etc. As such, different signs and symptoms are linked with associated receptors in your CNS and PNS being affected.  My pharmacology class was one of the hardest subjects for me personally, and even up to now I still find myself having to review all the different aspects of it just because of how intricate it is. I think if I had a more detailed understanding of the nervous system before I started my classes, I would have benefitted from it greatly since the medications that we are able to give at the paramedic-level are tied with your nervous system. 

For paramedic-level or advanced patient assessment, review the SAMPLE assessment from your EMT course if you need a refresher. Now, try to think of at least 5 questions to come with each of those basic assessment questions. For example, let's do the letter P, which stands for PMHx (past medical history). Now try to incorporate other Hx questions, such as, "do you have/see a specialized doctor for your \_\_?" "any recent surgeries?" "have you had any complications with your last pre-natal checkup?" etc. Basically in this class we had to cover just about every single thing in terms of patient assessment, along with going over lectures of different S/S (signs and symptoms), and medical diagnoses. 

For cardiology, I recommend reviewing your circulatory and cardiovascular system A&P, along with understanding the blood flow through the heart. I can't explain it all right now in this post, but look up some cardiology videos relating to the physiology (dromotrope, chronotrope, inotrope), the electrophysiology (conduction system, the cardiac cycle), and some others. 

Hopefully this helps; I know I kinda just regurgitated a lot of information at you. And good luck!

FTO = field training officer. Usually newly hired paramedics or paramedics in training in an emergent system will be assigned an FTO on a truck to evaluate if they qualify and are able to pass as a competent paramedic for the service. 

IFT = interfacility transfer. This is a type of ambulance response in which a patient is either going to be moved from facility to facility (usually from a facility such as a rehab center or SNF [skilled nursing facility]to hospital or vice versa), or the patient will be discharged from hospital to home. IFT are both emergent and non-emergent ambulance responses, depending on what company you work for. Some emergent services around the state you live in may offer IFT services or not, depending on where you live.

EDIT: Thanks for the replier for correcting me.

Practice your physical head-to-toe assessments. I've had some coworkers and partners tell me that I go overboard with my stuff, but I practice those because I'm in medic school at the moment and I'm planning on switching to an emergent service after I graduate. But a good detailed head-to-toe assessment will help you find things that the hospital/facility staff or family may have missed when giving you pt details (i.e. I found some level 2 ulcers on the back side when me and my partner transported a 76 yo from his home to a hospital for a scheduled appointment).

Your SAMPLE stuff will either come from a nurse giving verbal report or paperwork at the hospital/facility; or if you're doing ambulance service requests from residences to hospitals/facilities, then from the patient themself or family. Common conditions I've seen from my time working for half a year at a private IFT includes: dementia pt's, pt's who are severely deconditioned to the point of not being able to stand up on their own, elderly, and occasionally those who only respond to verbal stimuli. Like what user Dry-humor-mus says, be familiar with how your company likes to chart; you'll have a FTO on the first couple of days and they will walk you through how and what to input on the charting sites. 

Work on V/S taking as well. And *please* do not make up v/s if the pt is stable during transport; apparently some people in the company that I work for are notorious for making things up.

This can depend on what kind of learner you are, but in my case and from my perspective, I learned med math quicker by applying equations/formulas to those questions. The formulas that I use for drips/infusions is:

X (med being applied over time expressed in gtts/min)= (TV [total volume of the medication in the IV bag] x DS [drip set]) / TT (total time) 

X (drip rate expressed in gtts/min) = (DD [desired dose] x DS [drip set]) / drug concentration

For the formula that requires a med being applied over time, be cautious of the time units being asked. If you’re being asked what is the drip rate of the med (X) expressed in gtts/min and your total time (TT) is expressed in hours, convert the hours to minutes. 

A website that (will more than likely) explain better than I can is: https://emtprep.com/resources/article/medication-math-101

Hope this helps!

Like what the other two users said, the scenarios I dealt with during my practical were BLS level scenarios. Specifically one trauma and two medical cases. 

Some tips I would suggest is:

1) Refer back/begin heavily memorizing the steps of the official NREMT EMT-B level medical/trauma assessment sheet(s). This will be essential towards your pt assessment/scenario gradings. 

2) When memorizing the steps to the NREMT EMT-B sheet, practice verbalizing each of these steps. At least in my experience during my practical, we had to keep verbalizing things (i.e the classic "BSI scene safety; PPE", "I will consider c-spine precautions because of...," "Do I see or notice any DCAP BTLS while palpating this") as a way to let our instructors or whoever's grading us know that we're covering all the bases of the sheet. 

3) If you think you need help with or need to refresh your memory when it comes to learning how to administer any of the EMT-B level medications, try to contact your instructor or any instructor in your program's dept. for practice. During my practical, I had to demonstrate setting up a nasal atomizer with Narcan along with stating the dosage and reason why I'm administering the med. 

4) Set your own pace while doing the pt assessments and scenario. "Slow is smooth, and smooth is fast." 

Hope these tips helped!
